chapter 05 · knowledge

Building a knowledge base for an agent

Chapter 00 said information reaches a prediction by exactly two routes: the weights, and the context. The weights are frozen and stale. This chapter is about the second route, engineered — and it opens with the question most teams skip: whether you need a vector store at all.

Take the concrete case: a few hundred papers as PDFs, fifty cloned repositories, an index describing them. The default move is to embed everything and call it RAG. That default is now a contestable design decision rather than the obvious answer, and the evidence for contesting it arrived recently.

01

Does an agent need embeddings, or a good index and grep?

A real question with recent measurements — and no settled answer.

The old framing was: a model cannot read a corpus, so retrieve the relevant pieces first. But an agent can read — it can run grep, open a file, follow a reference, and try again. That changes the question from "which chunks are nearest?" to "what interface does the model get to the corpus?"

for grep

Direct Corpus Interaction — an agent searching raw files with terminal tools, no embedding model, no vector index, no retrieval API.

Reports beating strong sparse, dense and reranking baselines on several BRIGHT and BEIR datasets, with competitive results on BrowseComp-Plus and multi-hop QA. Headline averages: +11.0% agentic search, +30.7% multi-hop QA, +21.5% IR ranking. No offline index, so it adapts to a corpus that changes. (Li et al., arXiv 2605.05242 — verified; code released)

for retrieval

Bounded cost. A retriever selects candidates once, cheaply.

An exploring agent scans repeatedly and pays in tool calls and latency. The follow-on work names exactly this — relevance-agnostic exploration is expensive — and proposes using relevance as a prior rather than abandoning retrieval.

Do not over-read this. It is one recent, credible research line — not settled production science, and not evidence that lexical exploration wins on every corpus or latency budget. What it does establish is that "obviously you need a vector database" is no longer a safe default, and that a grep-over-a-good-index baseline is a real baseline you are obliged to beat rather than skip.

So the design that follows is neither pure: a navigable corpus first, retrieval added as candidate generation — not as a gate every piece of evidence must pass through.

02

Why not just put it all in the window?

Sometimes you should. The limit is price, not principle.

"RAG only exists because context windows were small" is too strong, but it is not empty — with a million-token window, a small stable corpus can simply be read.

FindingVerdict
Comprehensive comparison, long context vs RAGLong context more accurate when adequately resourced; RAG substantially cheaper
A 2025 re-evaluationWinner depends on structure: long context generally better on Wikipedia-style QA, summarization-based retrieval comparable, chunk retrieval worse, RAG better for dialogue and general queries
Practical thresholdUnder ~200k tokens, prompting the whole thing is reasonable — especially with caching

The economics are the real constraint. A corpus sent repeatedly is priced at corpus scale on every call; retrieval sends a small selection plus the cost of selecting. For a few hundred PDFs — comfortably millions of tokens — whole-corpus prompting is not the answer, but whole-document reads after navigation usually are. Find the paper, then read the paper.

03

Chunking is an information-loss decision

Not a parameter. Choose what you are willing to destroy.

Every chunking strategy severs something. The only question is what, and whether it is something your questions depend on.

StrategyWhat it destroys
Fixed token windowsSplits a Methods argument mid-logic; separates a caption from its figure and a table from its header
Sentence / semantic boundariesIsolates anaphora — "this approach", "the former", with the referent in another chunk
Section chunksCoherent, but dilutes: one relevant sentence in 2 000 words of context
Parent–childRetrieve the small child, read the parent section. Costs an index; usually worth it
Contextual retrievalPrepend generated context to each chunk. Vendor reports 49% fewer failed retrievals, 67% with reranking — vendor-reported, reproduce on your own corpus
Late chunkingEmbed the long document, then pool into chunks. More efficient; an independent comparison finds a trade-off, not a free win

For scientific papers this is not an abstract concern. The things you most want to retrieve are precisely the things chunking breaks: a Methods paragraph whose meaning depends on the sentence before it, a figure caption divorced from its figure, a parameter in a supplementary table. Treat PDF extraction as a measured upstream model, not plumbing — keep page coordinates, captions, tables and the original file, and evaluate the extractor on your own papers before trusting anything downstream of it.

04

The design that follows

A navigable corpus, with retrieval as one tool among several.
  1. Make the corpus navigable before making it searchable. Stable identifiers (document, version, page, section), canonical metadata in an index the agent can read, extracted text beside the original PDF, rendered page and figure assets. Most retrieval problems are organization problems wearing a costume.
  2. Give the agent file tools. find, grep/rg, metadata filter, targeted read, open-the-original-page. This is the baseline everything else must beat.
  3. Add retrieval as candidate generation. Lexical search for exact identifiers — gene names, accessions, flags, API symbols, error strings, where embeddings are actively bad. Dense retrieval for paraphrase and concept discovery. Fuse, rerank, then let the agent read the source.
  4. Make every claim resolve to a span. A citation that points to a document is not provenance; one that points to a page and offset is. This is what catches the failure below.
  5. Evaluate retrieval separately from answering. Recall@k on questions you wrote with known answers, before any end-to-end number. Otherwise a good answer hides a bad retrieval and a bad answer blames the wrong stage.

The failure mode with no analogue in ordinary search: the retriever and the reader are the same probabilistic system, so the agent can produce a fluent, correct-sounding answer grounded in the wrong chunk — and it will cite that chunk, confidently. Nothing in the pipeline raises an error. The only defence is provenance precise enough that you can check, cheaply, whether the cited span actually says what the answer claims.

Exercise p4 — beat the baseline or admit it won. Build against a real corpus, and make the comparison honest.

StepWhat it establishes
Write 20 questions with known answers, before building anythingthe eval exists before the thing it judges — and cannot be tuned to fit
Baseline: agent + grep + index + file readsthe number everything else must beat
Add lexical retrieval, then dense, then rerankingwhat each stage is actually worth on your corpus
Score retrieval and answering separatelywhich stage fails when the whole thing does
Check whether cited spans support the answersthe right-answer-wrong-chunk rate — the number nobody reports

You can now say, for a given corpus, which retrieval design you would build and what measurement would show it beats grep over a good index — and you know the failure mode that measurement has to catch.
